cards.h: From one-party dominance to a messy democracy
cards.b: The 1960s to 80s saw wars, economic crisis, Indira Gandhi’s rise, the Emergency and the first non-Congress governments. UPSC loves cause-and-effect here.

Nehru died on 27 May 1964. Lal Bahadur Shastri became PM; the Green Revolution and the White Revolution (Verghese Kurien’s Operation Flood, 1970) began. The 1965 war with Pakistan (Operation Gibraltar; Rann of Kutch; ceasefire; Tashkent Declaration, 10 January 1966; Shastri died there). The 1966 devaluation of the rupee and drought hurt.

cards.h: Indira Gandhi and the Congress split
cards.b: Indira Gandhi became PM in January 1966 (“goongi gudiya”). 1967 elections: Congress lost seats and eight states; coalitions (SVD governments) appeared. 1969: Congress split (Syndicate vs Indira); bank nationalisation (14 banks), the privy purse abolition attempt; “Garibi Hatao” (1971 election, big win). 1971: Bangladesh war; the Shimla Agreement (1972). 1974: first nuclear test at Pokhran (“Smiling Buddha”).

cards.h: The JP movement and the Emergency
cards.b: Navnirman (Gujarat) and the Bihar movement (1974); Jayaprakash Narayan’s call for “total revolution”. Allahabad High Court (12 June 1975, Justice Sinha) found Indira guilty of electoral malpractice (Raj Narain case). Emergency proclaimed 25 June 1975 under Article 352 (internal disturbance): opponents jailed, press censored, MISA, forced sterilisation (Sanjay Gandhi), slum demolitions. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended the Lok Sabha term to six years and added “socialist”, “secular”, Fundamental Duties.

Emergency lifted 21 March 1977. In the 1977 election the Janata Party won; Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress PM. The Shah Commission. The 44th Amendment (1978) made “internal disturbance” into “armed rebellion” and restored rights. Janata collapsed; Charan Singh briefly; Indira returned in January 1980. Punjab militancy; Operation Blue Star (June 1984); assassination of Indira Gandhi (31 October 1984) and anti-Sikh riots. Rajiv Gandhi won 1984 with 400-plus seats.

Rajiv’s early reforms: anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985), Assam and Punjab accords, telecom and computers. Controversies: the Shah Bano case and the Muslim Women Act (1986), Ayodhya locks opened, Bofors, IPKF in Sri Lanka (1987 to 90). 1989: V. P. Singh’s National Front; Mandal Commission recommendations (7 August 1990; 27% OBC reservation). Rath Yatra (L. K. Advani, 1990). Chandra Shekhar (1990 to 91) and the foreign exchange crisis. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991. Narasimha Rao and liberalisation followed.

Green Revolution (M. S. Swaminathan, Norman Borlaug; HYV wheat in Punjab, Haryana, west UP); food self-sufficiency by the late 1970s. Planning slowed; the oil shocks (1973, 1979) and balance of payments strains. Rise of regional parties (DMK, Akali Dal, TDP in 1982, AGP 1985) and social movements (Chipko, Dalit Panthers 1972, farmers).

cards.h: Emergency: aberration or logic of centralisation?
cards.b: Supporters said it restored order; critics call it the darkest chapter. Scholars (Rudolph and Rudolph, Granville Austin) see a crisis of institutions and the personalisation of power. The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) and the ADM Jabalpur case (1976, widely seen as wrong; overruled in effect by Puttaswamy, 2017) are central. Some say the 1989 shift began coalition politics.

25 June is observed as “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas” (since 2024). The Basic Structure doctrine, press freedom and anti-defection law (10th Schedule) come from this era. Coalition governments from 1989 to 2014 shaped federalism and policy, before the BJP’s 2014 majority. The Mandal debate continues in caste census talks.
